summary:
Saint Kitts and Nevis no longer criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. On 29 August 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Jamal Jeffers v The Attorney General, struck sections 56 (buggery) and 57 (indecent assault against men) of the Offences Against the Person Act as contrary to the constitutional rights to privacy and freedom of expression. The ruling took immediate effect and decriminalised consensual sexual intercourse between adult men in private across the country. Consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful since that judgment.

The decriminalisation came through a civil-society constitutional challenge rather than legislation, and the judgment was issued by a regional court whose rulings also affected neighbouring Eastern Caribbean states. Human Dignity Trust and 76 Crimes track the wider pattern of regional challenges to anti-sodomy laws, of which this case formed part.

Legal gender recognition is not available. No statute, court process or administrative route in Saint Kitts and Nevis allows a person to obtain official recognition of a changed gender marker, and the sources document no pending reform.

No provision of the penal code or of any other statute prohibits discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Discrimination in the workplace, in education and in accommodation remains lawful, as does hate speech directed at LGBT people. Same-sex unions are not recognised in any form, whether as marriage or as a registered partnership, and same-sex households receive none of the rights available to opposite-sex married couples.

Official hostility is on record. In 2011 the Government of Saint Kitts and Nevis stated that it had no mandate from the people to abolish criminalisation of homosexuality among consenting adults. In 2005 the port authority of Nevis barred a cruise ship carrying 110 passengers, most of them gay, from docking; a police boat intercepted the vessel and it was ordered to sail on, with port officials describing the exclusion as a decision that homosexuality was not to be part of the island's culture. Civil society reports that LGBT people in the country avoid law enforcement, which limits the practical value of the 2022 judgment as a protection mechanism.
tangentialFactors:
The 2022 judgment belongs to a regional wave of constitutional litigation against anti-sodomy statutes in the Eastern Caribbean. Reporting by Nation News and tracking by 76 Crimes and Human Dignity Trust place Saint Kitts and Nevis among several Caribbean nations targeted by such lawsuits, so the legal framework here is shared in origin with neighbouring jurisdictions and could be revisited by a higher or differently composed court.

The 2005 exclusion of a cruise ship from Nevis stands as the clearest documented instance of entry being refused on explicitly anti-gay grounds. The interception by a police boat and the public framing of the decision by port officials indicate that discretionary port and immigration authority has previously been exercised against LGBT arrivals.

Anti-discrimination coverage in the region is uneven, and the absence of any sexual-orientation or gender-identity clause in Saint Kitts and Nevis is consistent with the position recorded for several neighbouring states rather than distinctive to this country.
localsOnly:
LGBTQ+ citizens are named within the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027, but civil-society submissions to the Universal Periodic Review in 2025 record a lack of tangible implementing steps by the State. The policy's inclusion of LGBTQ+ people has not produced statutory protections.

LGBTI organisations are able to register and operate in Saint Kitts and Nevis, and domestic civil-society groups, working with a regional alliance, brought the case that produced the 2022 decriminalisation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory confirms whether any hate-crime sentencing enhancement exists or has been applied to offences against LGBT people; the sources address only the general absence of non-discrimination and harassment provisions, and this remains unresolved.

Procedures for amending gender markers on passports, national identification or birth records are not sourced. The inventory states that legal gender recognition is not possible but does not document the administrative practice of the passport office or the registry, and the position on secondary documents is unresolved.

No sourced information addresses whether the 2022 judgment altered police handling of complaints by LGBT complainants, or whether any training, guidance or oversight mechanism was issued after it. The claim that LGBT people avoid law enforcement rests on civil-society reporting and is not accompanied by incident-level data.
